documents.title: The strange economics of free concerts
documents.text:
In many cities, summer brings a season of free outdoor concerts, funded by councils that regard them as a gift to residents. Yet the arrangement is less simple than it appears, and a recent study of twelve such programs suggests that the benefits are distributed rather differently from what organizers assume.

The authors found that the audiences were not, in the main, the poorer residents for whom free events are often justified. Attendees were typically older, better educated and more likely to live near the venue than the city as a whole. Surveys suggested that many were drawn less by the music than by the pleasure of an unplanned evening in good company, which is not something that price alone can create.

The programs, however, delivered other returns. Restaurants within walking distance reported a rise in evening trade of around fifteen percent on concert nights, and the council's own accounts suggested that the extra spending more than offset the cost of the event. Organizers who had hoped to broaden the audience therefore faced an awkward finding: the concerts were good for business, though less successful as a social program.

The researchers do not recommend ending the events. They suggest instead that councils spend part of the budget on transport and publicity aimed at neighborhoods that currently stay away.

questions.prompt: What is the main finding of the study?
choices: Free concerts attract mainly younger residents
Concerts lose money for nearby restaurants
Free concerts reach a narrower audience
Residents dislike outdoor evening events
questions.explanation: The audience was older, better educated and local, not the poorer residents.

questions.prompt: What economic benefit did the programs bring?
choices: Higher evening takings at nearby cafes
Lower costs for the council's transport
Rising ticket sales for later concerts
More jobs in the local music industry
questions.explanation: Restaurants reported evening trade up around fifteen percent.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the audience's motives?
choices: Most came for the free refreshments on offer
Few of them knew the concerts were free
Most were paid by the event organizers
Many came for the evening more than the music
questions.explanation: Many were drawn by an unplanned evening in good company.

questions.prompt: What do the researchers recommend?
choices: Charging a modest fee to all attendees
Keep the events but reach other areas
Cancelling the concerts altogether
Moving the events to the city center
questions.explanation: They suggest spending on transport and publicity for neighborhoods that stay away.

documents.title: Declining an invitation to join an advisory board
documents.text:
To: Professor Margaret Oduya, Chair, Advisory Board
From: Rafael Domínguez
Subject: Your invitation to join the board

Dear Professor Oduya,

Thank you very much for your invitation to join the advisory board of the Institute. I am honored by the offer, and I have given it more thought than my brief reply on Monday may have suggested.

After considering the matter carefully, I have concluded that I cannot accept at present. The reasons are practical, not a reflection on the Institute's work, which I greatly admire. In January I will assume the directorship of my own organization, and I expect that my first year will require nearly all of my attention. To join your board and attend only half the meetings would, I feel, be unfair to you and a poor use of the seat.

I should like to suggest that you consider my colleague, Dr. Ingrid Salomonsen, who has the expertise in public finance that your board has said it lacks. I have already mentioned the possibility to her, and she has expressed interest, though she has not yet seen the details.

If the invitation could be renewed in two years, I would be delighted to reconsider. In the meantime, I hope I may remain in touch, and I would be happy to help informally if the Institute should need advice.

With sincere thanks,
Rafael Domínguez

To resign from his own directorship
questions.explanation: He declines the invitation and proposes Dr. Salomonsen.

documents.title: Introduction of a new expense card system
documents.text:
MEMORANDUM
To: All managers
From: Ibrahim Nasser, Chief Financial Officer
Subject: Replacement of the petty cash system by company cards

From 1 November, petty cash boxes will be withdrawn from all offices and replaced by company expense cards, which will be issued to team leaders and to employees who travel regularly.

The decision follows an internal review which found that handling cash consumed roughly two hours of administrative time per office each week and that discrepancies, though small, occurred in almost every audit. Cards will make each purchase traceable and will allow the finance team to see spending as it happens, rather than at the end of the month.

Each card will carry a monthly limit set by the department head, and purchases will be restricted to approved categories such as travel, meals and office supplies. Cardholders must photograph each receipt and upload it to the expense app within five working days; transactions without receipts will be deducted from the cardholder's next salary payment.

I recognize that some staff will find the new rules more demanding than the old arrangement. A short training session will be offered in every office during October, and a help desk will operate until the end of the year. Questions about eligibility should be sent to my assistant, Ms. Quill.

choices: Receipts will no longer be required
Managers will lose all spending authority
Travel will be banned for most staff
Cash boxes give way to company cards
questions.explanation: Petty cash is replaced by expense cards.

questions.prompt: Why did the review recommend the change?
choices: Cash had been stolen from several offices

The bank had raised its handling fees
questions.explanation: Handling cash took about two hours a week and discrepancies occurred in almost every audit.

questions.explanation: Transactions without receipts will be deducted from the next salary payment.

questions.explanation: Cards go to team leaders and to employees who travel regularly; eligibility questions go to Ms. Quill.

documents.title: Ferndale Language Institute: learn by living the language
documents.text:
Most language courses promise fluency and deliver a vocabulary list. At the Ferndale Language Institute, we begin from a different assumption: that a language is learned by using it, and that the best classroom is a conversation.

Our intensive courses, offered in six languages, run for four weeks and are limited to eight students per group. Mornings are devoted to structured lessons, but afternoons are spent on projects in the real world: ordering at a market, negotiating a rental, or interviewing a local resident for a short film. Teachers are native speakers, and all instruction after the first week takes place in the target language.

We do not pretend that the method is easy. Students who have followed our courses report that the first fortnight can be tiring, since it demands constant concentration. Our records, however, show that three quarters of participants advance a full level on the international scale within a month, compared with the usual two or three months in a conventional course.

Fees start at 1,900 dollars and include lodging with a local host family. Scholarships covering up to forty percent of the fee are awarded each term to applicants under twenty-five. To book a place, or to arrange a trial lesson, visit our office or write to admissions.

questions.explanation: It stresses conversation and real-world projects.

questions.explanation: Afternoons are devoted to projects such as ordering at a market or interviewing residents.

documents.title: Letter responding to a student's appeal
documents.text:
Dear Ms. Varga,

I write on behalf of the Examinations Board in response to your appeal, received on 12 June, against the grade awarded for your dissertation. I have read your submission carefully, together with the original markers' reports and the comments of the external examiner.

The Board has concluded that the mark of sixty-two percent should stand. You argue that the first marker failed to take account of the difficulty of obtaining interview data from a hospital that withdrew its cooperation midway through your research. I accept that this was a serious obstacle, and the Board has noted that you handled it with considerable resourcefulness. However, the regulations do not permit the mark to be adjusted for circumstances of this kind; they allow adjustment only where there has been an error in the process or evidence of bias, and the Board found neither.

I should add that both markers praised the clarity of your argument and the quality of your analysis, and that the lower mark reflects chiefly the small size of the sample, which limited the strength of your conclusions.

If you wish, you may ask for a written explanation of how the mark was calculated, and you may also apply for a further review, within twenty-eight days, on the ground that the process was irregular. I am sorry that I cannot give you a more favorable outcome.

Yours sincerely,
Dr. Leonie Whitcombe, Secretary to the Board

documents.title: The unfinished business of the paperless ballot
documents.text:
Several countries have in recent years moved toward electronic voting, attracted by the promise of faster counts and fewer spoiled ballots. The experience of the northern republic, which introduced touch-screen machines three elections ago, suggests that the transition is less straightforward than advocates predicted.

The machines have indeed reduced the time taken to announce results, from about nine hours to two. Spoiled ballots have almost disappeared, since the machines warn voters of errors. But security specialists have raised a serious objection: the machines produce no paper record, so that, in the event of a dispute, there is nothing to recount. An audit commissioned by the electoral commission found no evidence of tampering, but it also admitted that, without a paper trail, such evidence could not easily have been found.

The government has promised a modification that will print a receipt, which the voter can check and deposit in a box. Critics welcome the idea but note that the change will cost more than the original machines, and that it may not be ready before the next election. Meanwhile, public trust, according to one poll, has fallen: sixty percent of voters say that they are not sure that their vote is counted accurately.

questions.explanation: The article weighs faster counts against the lack of a paper record.

questions.prompt: What improvement did the machines bring?

documents.title: Returns and exchanges at Lindqvist Outdoor
documents.text:
Can I return an item? Yes. Unworn and unused items may be returned within thirty days of delivery for a full refund, provided that they are in their original packaging and that all tags are attached. Footwear that has been worn outdoors cannot be accepted.

Who pays for the return? If the item is faulty or was sent in error, we cover the cost of postage and will email you a prepaid label. In all other cases, the customer pays the return postage, which is deducted from the refund unless the order exceeded 150 dollars.

How long does a refund take? Once the parcel reaches our warehouse, we inspect the goods within three working days and refund the payment within a further five. The time that the money takes to appear in your account depends on your bank.

Can I exchange an item for a different size? Yes, provided the new size is in stock. Exchanges are shipped free of charge, but we cannot reserve a size before we have received the original item. If you are in a hurry, you may prefer to return the item for a refund and place a fresh order.

Sale items are final and cannot be returned unless they are faulty.
